title: Several Waymo Self-Driving Cars Stalled in Traffic as San Francisco's Streets Flooded
description:
San Francisco's streets flooded this week after heavy rainfall — confusing several Waymo self-driving cars. The San Francisco blog Sfist describes what happened after the flooding in some places rose as high as three feet:
Two lanes of Oak Street by the Golden Gate Park Panhandle were flooded Wednesday morning, with water spouting out of manhole covers, leading to a traffic backup that was made worse by a Waymo that couldn't figure its way out of the situation. The Waymo vehicle came to a stop in front of the spouting water, blocking one of the only passable lanes and worsening the traffic situation, as seen in the video below that is going viral... ["Other drivers had to veer into deeper water to weave around it," reports the San Francisco Chronicle.] 


Elsewhere in the city, Waymo rider Edward Frazer posted the video below to X, also around 10:20 am, saying that he had been in a Waymo for an hour and a half trying to get from North Beach to Mission Bay, with the vehicle pulling over around 10 times as it encountered flooded streets. The video shows the Waymo on what appears to be Townsend Street near Adobe's headquarters, stalled as water puddles in front of it. 
Waymo subsequently suspended all service for the rest of the day. 

But "frozen robotaxis were already clogging San Francisco streets by the time Waymo decided to rein in the fleet," reports the San Francisco Chronicle:

 Rider Amy Gutierrez said her Waymo suddenly stopped on Fell Street at the intersection of Masonic Avenue, where rain was coursing into rivers. She contacted company support and was transferred to three specialists who tried to move the jammed vehicle. It took a half-hour of false starts before they managed to remotely maneuver it to the right lane. "We were kind of just stuck there — cars were honking," she said, and other drivers were frustrated as traffic backed up. "One person drove by smacking their window, like 'Get out of the way.'" 
Or, as the New York Post puts it, "Waymos spark terror as they trap drivers in rapidly rising floodwater as monster storm hits California city."

Waymos have sparked chaos in San Francisco as they trapped passengers in cars despite rapidly rising floods. Multiple self-driving vehicles were paralyzed across the streets and left those inside frantically calling the company to help get them to safety.
One was trapped in the middle of a busy intersection when the car refused to go around an overflowing drain, leaving other drivers to go on the wrong side of the road to get around.... 

The San Francisco Chronicle also remembers that last year's power blackout caused 1,600 Waymo vehicles to stall "because they required a 'confirmation check' from a human operator before navigating stoplights after the power was cut. Hundreds of requests overwhelmed the system, leaving San Francisco streets full of paralyzed self-driving vehicles." 

Thanks to Slashdot reader AzWa Snowbird for sharing the news.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: US DOJ Charges Suspected Russian Agent for Stalking Palantir Employees in California
description:
America's Justice Department is prosecuting a suspected foreign agent in "a state-sponsored operation" that targeted tech workers in Palo Alto, California. "We will not tolerate any efforts — by foreign governments or otherwise — to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," said U.S. Attorney Craig H. Missakian. 

The alleged Russian agent was arrested in October for "stalking and harassing employees of the software and AI firm Palantir, sources told ABC News, because of its assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."

 The indictment says D'iu traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City last June and was connected with a person who helped him illegally cross the southern U.S. border. Once in the U.S., he was instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones and remote access software that his co-conspirators used to help him in his alleged targeting of the company's employees. At one point, prosecutors say D'iu was directed by his co-conspirators to visit a coffee shop where many of the company's employees would work and try to identify them and take pictures of their screens while they were working... 

In September, prosecutors say D'iu allegedly followed a female employee of the company in his vehicle for nearly 30 miles after she left the company's Palo Alto, California, office. Even as the employee attempted various maneuvers to evade him, D'iu aggressively sought to follow her until she ultimately phoned police and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco Police Department's Mission Station.
 

The nonprofit news site Palo Alto Online notes the government's affidavit "identified at least two other instances in early September in which employees of the defense company reported being followed by a car matching the description of D'iu's silver Lexus SUV.

The coffee shops and other locations where D'iu stationed his laptop — sometimes for hours at a time — are in close proximity to the Palantir office in downtown Palo Alto... FBI agents executed a search warrant on Oct. 8 at D'iu's residence in East Palo Alto. There they found the California state ID, passport and Social Security card that were present in the DHL packages, as well as two Russian passports, $18,000 in cash and a notebook with 10 Palo Alto area addresses. Five of them correlate to the home addresses of employees at the unnamed Silicon Valley defense company. The agents also recovered three employee "target package profiles" that included their names, names of relatives, education and employment history, leadership qualities and a list of strengths and weaknesses. 

After searching D'iu's phone, the FBI found messages from a Telegram contact with photos of four employees and their addresses. D'iu was instructed to act like a food delivery driver and knock on their doors to verify if the employees did live at those addresses, according to the affidavit... 

If convicted of all charges, D'iu could face a cumulative maximum sentence of 21 years in federal prison and $850,000 in fines.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: 59 Years Later, 'The Prisoner' is Getting a Second Remake - from Amazon Studios
description:
The Prisoner is getting a remake, reports ScreenRant. "Amazon Studios is currently developing a new and modern twist on the short-lived series..."

ITV only aired 17 episodes of the original Prisoner back in 1967 and 1968, but it did receive a nomination for Best Dramatic Presentation at the Hugo Awards. Reviews were overwhelmingly positive... The Prisoner, considered one of the greatest sci-fi fantasy TV shows of all time, currently holds a perfect score among critics on Rotten Tomatoes and a 93% with audiences. 

You can watch all 17 original episodes on YouTube. And apparently the production team for the remake "is apparently full of fans of the initial series," writes Inverse, citing an article from The Hollywood Reporter, "and ITV, the British TV network, is on board as well, which lends a little credence to it." 

More details on the remake from ScreenRant:
 Susan Montford, Don Murphy, Philippe Maigret, and Lucienne Papon have signed on as executive producers, but a showrunner has not been selected yet... Murphy has produced every single live-action Transformers movie, as well as the animated flick Transformers One. He also worked with Montford on Real Steel, Shoot 'Em Up, While She Was Out, and Vampire Academy... There have been attempts in the past to create a movie based on The Prisoner, with big names like Christopher Nolan, Ridley Scott, and Simon West all interested at various points, but nothing ever materialized... 

It took 41 years after the end of The Prisoner for any remake to finally make it to air. The six-episode 2009 miniseries had a solid cast that included Ian McKellen... McKellen and cinematographer Florian Hoffmeister even scored Emmy nominations. Unfortunately, reviews weren't kind to the show, which has a very low 17% critic score and 41% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. 
Thanks to Slashdot reader joshuark for sharing the news.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Americans Enters Post-Penny World, Businesses Now Allowed to Round Cash Transactions to Nearest Nickel
description:
Friday U.S. President Trump "signed the Common Cents Act, which now lets businesses round cash transactions to the nearest nickel, into law," reports CBS News:

It sets standards for cash transactions that businesses and consumers can use when exact change isn't available, as the penny is phased out. The legislation calls for cash transactions to be rounded up or down to the nearest 5 cents... Before its passage, businesses could be sued if they failed to give customers exact change, even when rounding up in a patron's favor. 
CBS includes this quote from an official NACS, an advocacy group for the convenience/fuel retailing industry. "Retailers have been looking for federal guidance on processing cash transactions since penny production ended. 

 NBC News points out that the U.S. Mint said it would still produce collector's versions of pennies in "limited quantities," reporting on what has and hasn't changed now:

The penny can still be used as legal tender "for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues," according to the new law. The Treasury Department said last year that the Federal Reserve will continue to recirculate the approximately 114 billion pennies that are in existence "for as long as possible...." And, as the nickel replaces the penny at the bottom of the U.S. Mint's currency list, that coin can now be manufactured with an inner layer of zinc and an outer layer of nickel [according to the newly-signed law]. It is currently produced with nickel and copper, which costs more than zinc.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Will AI-Fueled Cyberattacks Lead to Better Funding for Critical Open Source Projects?
description:
Remember that famous XKCD comic joking that all modern digital infrastructure rests on "a project some random person in Nebraska has been thanklessly maintaining since 2003." 

Politico Europe's cybersecurity reporter wonders if this recent spate of outages suggests that supporting block is coming loose? (Especially after Politico reported Thursday that internal services at EU institutions went offline after a major AI-fueled cyberattack.)

Authorities blame the sudden wave of instability on the capacity of new AI tools to detect vulnerabilities in existing code and for bad actors to exploit them... Interviews with more than a dozen cybersecurity leaders and those working on maintaining the internet show the scale of the challenge to keep the web up and running, in a world where the pace of finding vulnerabilities has rapidly and permanently accelerated. Since the web's early days, an unruly cast of idealist engineers and non-profit foundations have been essential for looking after decades-old critical code that's been used to build our digital world. This small army of largely volunteer coders now say they can't keep up with the power and pace of AI. "We're running on fumes," said Robin Bender Ginn, executive director of the OpenJS Foundation, which looks after JavaScript, among the most widely used programming languages. "It keeps me up at night." 


Cybersecurity agencies around the world rang the alarm last month about major flaws detected in PHP, another critical coding language that underpins 70% of the web. This week, similar scares have spread over Java and NGINX, which also fuel large swathes of technology. Helmut Reisinger, the European chief executive of cybersecurity giant Palo Alto Networks, said in an interview that the company is seeing "more or less" ten times as many incidents compared to about four months ago. He predicts the constant drumbeat of attacks and scares in the last month is going to become the "new norm...." 


The rise of AI models and their capabilities of finding software flaws is putting more pressure on open-source software engineers, who are inundated with reports of vulnerabilities — some of which are false or exaggerated. Reports of flaws discovered by AI are "quite verbose," Ginn said. Juhan Lepassaar, the head of EU cyber agency ENISA, said in an interview that the agency has observed a similar pattern of false positives. 

While some hope the AI-fueled attacks "will put the needs of open source software on the map and prompt an intervention," according to the article, "many of those steeped in the ecosystem... have their doubts." 

"I'm a bit pessimistic," says Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member. "I worry that people will just not care enough to actually do anything about it."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Nvidia's Accounting Practices Now Being Investigated by America's SEC
description:
We knew America's Securities and Exchange Commission was investigating Nvidia.
But Reuters reported Friday that what's being investigated is Nvidia's accounting practices, according to "two people briefed on the matter."


Prices of Nvidia shares extended losses and were down about 13% on Friday, according to LSEG data, after Reuters reported details of the SEC probe. They had been down more than 6% before Reuters published its report... The SEC probe is the latest of Nvidia's legal woes. The Justice Department has also been reviewing Nvidia's $12.9-billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face alongside a broader antitrust investigation into the company's acquisitions and practices, Reuters reported last month. 

Reuters says they "could not immediately determine" exactly what potential accounting issues America's SEC is examining." (And Reuters points out that "Investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and many close without resulting in enforcement action.") 

Their article adds some historical context — that U.S. authorities "have been investigating Megaspeed since 2024 over possible violations of export controls related to alleged shipments of Nvidia AI chips to China, the US Justice and Commerce departments said this week." And the Financial Times reported Tuesday that Nvidia removed Singapore from its geographical breakdown of revenue sources, Reuters points out, "even as Singapore sales soared to almost half its global revenue."

Analysts and investors have also grown increasingly concerned about circular AI financing deals, in which chipmakers including Nvidia have pursued complex financial arrangements to help customers fund purchases of their chips and the construction of costly AI infrastructure, such as data centers... Speaking to Reuters last month, SEC enforcement chief David Woodcock said the agency was examining AI companies' corporate disclosures to ensure issuers are giving investors the full picture on potential risks. On its Tuesday earnings call, Nvidia's interim CEO and former CFO Colette Kress said the company was proud of its role in supporting the AI industry, but would be far more selective moving forward about AI industry financing deals.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Earth has a New Moon
description:
"Earth is currently hosting a second moon," reports CNN:

Our planet's gravity captured the tiny asteroid in April. This temporary "mini-moon" — about 2 meters (6 feet) in diameter — will stick around until early December, when it's expected to leave Earth's sphere of influence and continue on a path around the sun. 

The object is so small and dim in observations that astronomers needed several weeks to confirm it wasn't a defunct satellite or a fragment of one. The International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center — which tracks asteroids, comets and other small bodies in the solar system — named the newcomer 2026 QQ8 in late October. 


While mini-moon is not an official designation, astronomers have previously used the moniker to characterize a handful of natural objects, including 2006 RH120, which spent around one year in Earth orbit, and 2020 CD3, which orbited our planet for about three years. However, it's not uncommon for Earth to have one of these transient companions. "On average, there's probably one there at any given time," said Matthew Payne, director of the Minor Planet Center. "They hang around for a few weeks or months. Sometimes it's none, sometimes it's a couple." The catalog of these visitors is relatively short because they usually slip under the radar... 

The exact origin of the space rock is "an active area of inquiry," Payne said, but most NEOs originate from the asteroid belt, a region between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter that contains millions of rocky objects of varying size that revolve around the sun. Over millions of years, gravitational forces can shift some of these objects' orbits toward the inner solar system.

title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
 
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED.
 
"We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
description:
A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports: A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins.
 
The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. 
"During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester.
 
"We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
description:
Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years. 

2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 
2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof 

Add a new headline to the list... 

2026: Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries 

joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
 
[...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...] Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...]
 
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."
"If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone."
 
"If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
 
In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system. 


But did a human beat the AI? The Washington Post reports:


Just hours after Alpoge's claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors. 
But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag. 

"If any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this," he wrote. "We are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere."







Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: FCC Backs AT&T's Plan To Remove Copper Landlines In California
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from PCMag: On Friday, the FCC announced that it was preempting "specific requirements in California law that prevent consumers from transitioning off of unreliable, slow copper lines," even as some residents fear they'll be saddled with spotty cell service as an alternative. AT&T argues that California's "Carrier of the Last Resort" (COLR) rules prevent it from removing the old-school copper network that currently serves only 3% of California households, a number that continues to shrink. In May, the company urged the commission to declare that federal laws preempted California's regulations, thus clearing the way for AT&T to discontinue the service as it prioritizes high-speed fiber and expanded 5G cellular coverage.
 
Friday's FCC order (PDF) partially grants AT&T's petition, agreeing that under federal law it has "explicit jurisdiction over the discontinuance of interstate telecommunications services." Still, the order refrains from "wholly" preempting California's Carrier of the Last Resort rules, and seems to instead focus on the AT&T situation. "While we preempt those requirements that necessitate that AT&T obtain a variety of CPUC [California Public Utilities Commission] approvals before it can discontinue POTS [plain old telephone service] in accordance with federal authorization, we do not preempt the COLR and other obligations more generally," the 74-page document says.
 
[...] Despite the FCC's order, it's not entirely clear if AT&T will pursue the copper landline phase-out in California. In May, the carrier sued to overturn the local regulations and block the CPUC from enforcing them against AT&T, which noted it spends $1 billion each year to maintain the copper network. That court case remains ongoing. [...] According to the regulator, AT&T has proposed discontinuing the legacy telephone service in the state on or after June 1, 2027.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: GTA 6 Hits Massive $3.79 Billion In First-Day Sales
description:
Rockstar Games' Grand Theft Auto VI generated a record-breaking $3.79 billion in preorders and first-day sales, making it the biggest entertainment launch in history, according to parent company Take-Two Interactive. The figure surpasses the lifetime global box-office earnings of Avengers: Endgame ($2.9 billion) and comes after more than a decade of development at a reported cost of $1.5 billion. The game developer declined to disclose the number of 'GTA 6' copies sold. 
"It is with immense gratitude that we enter a new chapter of Rockstar Games with the release of 'Grand Theft Auto VI,'" Rockstar Games president and founder Sam Houser said. "We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn't be more excited to share this moment with you."
 
Further reading: Gamers Skip Work to Play GTA VI After 13-Year Wait





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages
description:
Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports: Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly.
 
[...] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.
